title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling playbook, benchmarks & runbooks
author: Maya Patel
content:
Overview

This document is the canonical reference for Redwood Inference's serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling strategy, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, standard runbooks for common incidents, release notes summary for major runtime releases, and a consolidated known-issues list. It is intended for engineers (runtime, infra, SRE), performance owners, and release managers.

Sections in this document:
1) Architecture overview
2) Kernel scheduling design and heuristics
3) Profiling playbook (how-to for a perf investigation)
4) Benchmarking suite and interpretation guide
5) Standard runtime runbooks (incidents & ops)
6) Release notes & upgrade guidance (summary)
7) Known issues and mitigations
8) Team wiki pointer, ownership, and escalation

---

1. Architecture overview

Short summary: The serving runtime is a GPU-optimized inference engine composed of a front-end router (request layer), a scheduler/orchestrator, worker pools (device-local executors), and a persistent control plane for model metadata, KV cache state, and rollout policies. The runtime is designed for low-latency single-stream generation and high-throughput batching with configurable trade-offs via per-route policies.

Key components:
- Router: HTTP/gRPC layer that authenticates and normalizes requests. Responsible for initial routing decisions (route -> model/variant + preferred pool).
- Scheduler/Orchestrator: Global component with short-lived leadership that assigns requests to workers, decides batching windows, and enforces latency SLOs. 
- Executors (workers): Per-GPU processes (or containers) that run the inference engine. Executors manage token-level KV cache, local micro-batches, and kernel invocation.
- Model Store & Catalog: Stores model artifacts, quantization profiles, and verified performance metadata (p99 latency profiles, memory working set).
- KV Cache Layer: Optional persistent prefix/KV cache that can be local (in-GPU) or remote (Redis-like). Used to speed repeated prefixes and reduce total token compute.

SLOs and targets (typical):
- P50 text-gen latency (1-128 tokens): 20-50ms for small models, 50-150ms for medium, variable for long context.
- P95 target: 2x P50 baseline.
- Throughput target (Dedicated pools): 5k-100k tokens/sec per pool depending on GPU class and batching policy.

Ownership and contacts:
- Runtime architecture: eng-serving-runtime core team
- Scheduler & kernel work: Runtime kernel team (pager: runtime-kernel-oncall)
- Benchmarks & profiling harness: Applied ML & Evals (contact: Jia Huang)

---

2. Kernel scheduling design and heuristics

Goals: maximize GPU utilization, respect per-request latency SLOs, avoid priority inversion, and keep memory pressure predictable.

Scheduling primitives:
- Micro-batching: Executors collect compatible requests for a short window (default 4ms) then run a single batched kernel invocation.
- Priority lanes: Requests are tagged by priority (latency-sensitive, standard, background). Higher-priority lanes use shorter batching windows and preempt lower-priority aggregation.
- Kernel selection: Scheduler selects between a family of kernels (e.g., fast attention vs. memory-optimized attention) based on current sequence length distribution, memory headroom, and model quantization profile.
- Warm pools & pre-allocation: For models with high cold-start cost, the scheduler maintains a small pool of warm executors pinned to that model.

Heuristics and thresholds (operative defaults):
- Max micro-batch window: 8ms for latency tier, 32ms for standard tier.
- Max micro-batch size: tuned per model; default 32 for small models, 8-16 for large-parameter models.
- Preemptive eviction: If GPU free memory < 600MB, evict least-recently-used cached KV segments and fall back to memory-optimized kernels.
- Kernel fallback policy: if p95 of recent invocations > configured SLO for 30s, automatically switch to an alternative kernel variant and trigger an alert to perf@.

Operational knobs (configurable per-route):
- batching_window_ms, max_micro_batch_size, priority_lane, prefer_quantized_kernels (true/false), max_concurrent_streams.

Tracing & telemetry: Every scheduling decision emits structured telemetry: request_id, model, sequence_length, wait_time_ms, batch_size, kernel_variant, kernel_latency_ms, gpu_mem_before/after. Use /dashboards/runtime-scheduler for visualization.

---

3. Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

When to run: increased p95 latency, unexpected throughput drop, OOMs, or kernel regressions after a release.

Preflight checklist:
- Confirm reproducible workload (sample requests or synthetic trace).
- Identify failing model + route and timeframe.
- Gather SLO baseline and compare to historical.

Investigation steps (ordered):
1) Surface metrics: p50/p95/p99, batch sizes, wait_time_ms, GPU utilization, mem pressure, scheduler telemetry for the time period.
2) Run the profiling harness (locally or in staging) using the same request distribution:
   - CLI: ./bin/rt-profile --model <model> --trace-file traces/trace.json --duration 60s --capture-kernels=true
   - Output: per-kernel latency, occupancy, cuBLAS/cuDNN kernel names, stream utilization.
3) Capture a GPU timeline (NVIDIA Nsight / nvprof equivalent in cloud): collection includes kernel start/end, SM occupancy, memory copies. Use the runtime's /profiling/export endpoint to capture artifact.
4) Correlate kernel-level hotspots with scheduling telemetry (e.g., long wait_time_ms + sudden large batch size indicates micro-batching window misconfiguration).
5) Test kernel variants: try memory-optimized and attention-optimized variants with controlled inputs. Record p50/p95 and memory usage.
6) If OOMs observed, enable quantized path (if model supports it) and repeat.
7) Triaging: if regression is tied to code change, mark the release and collect repro for engineering.

Outputs to produce for every profiling run:
- One-page summary (what changed, hypothesis, key metric diffs)
- Profiling artifacts (gpu_timeline.zip, kernel_stats.csv) uploaded to /artifacts/serving-profiles/<run-id>
- Suggested mitigations and follow-up actions with owners and ETA.

---

4. Benchmarking suite & interpretation guide

Purpose: validate throughput/latency claims for new kernels, model quantization profiles, and dedicated pool instance types. Benchmarks are deterministic scripts that run range of sequence lengths and batch sizes.

Benchmark categories:
- Latency microbench: single-stream generation at sequence lengths [8, 32, 128, 512]. Reports p50/p95/p99 and kernel breakdown.
- Throughput sweep: increasing concurrent streams and batch sizes to map throughput vs latency curve.
- Cold-start & warm-up: measure the first-request latency after model load, and time to steady-state.
- Quantization impact: compare fp16 vs int8 or 4-bit variants for per-token latency and quality (using eval prompts).

How to run (example):
- ./bench/run_bench.sh --model <model> --gpu-type a100-40gb --suite latency,throughput --out results/<model>-<gpu>-<ts>.json

Interpreting results (guidance):
- Use p95 as the primary regressions gate for latency. If p95 increases by >10% from baseline for a released kernel, block rollout and trigger perf-rollback.
- Throughput regressions: compare area-under-curve (AUC) across batch sizes. A drop >15% triggers investigation.
- Quantization: measure quality degradation via eval set; a drop >1.5% absolute in key eval metrics requires product sign-off.

Artifact storage and dashboards:
- All benchmark results must be uploaded to /bench-results and cataloged in the Bench DB (internal). Dashboards: /dashboards/bench-overview and /dashboards/quantization-impact.

---

5. Standard runtime runbooks (operational playbooks)

Runbook: High p95 latency (stable production)
- Summary: sustained p95 elevation across a pool or route.
- Immediate checks:
  1. Confirm scope: single route, pool, region, or global.
  2. Check scheduler dashboard for unusual batch sizes or long wait_time_ms.
  3. Check GPU mem usage, OOM events, and kernel error codes.
  4. If recent runtime release (within 30m), consider automatic rollback to previous kernel image.
- Mitigation steps:
  - For scheduler misconfig: increase priority lane capacity or reduce batching_window_ms. Owner: runtime-scheduler team.
  - For kernel regression: set kernel_variant_override to previous stable variant and file a perf incident. Owner: runtime-kernel.
  - For capacity-induced tail latency: scale pool capacity (horizontal) or divert traffic to compatible region. Owner: SRE.

Runbook: OOM on executor
- Immediate: mark executor as unhealthy and remove from pool.
- Check: model size, max_batch_size, current KV cache occupancy.
- Quick fixes: reduce max_micro_batch_size for that route; enable quantized variant; restart executor with controlled memory flags.
- Longer-term: increase eviction aggressiveness for KV cache and tune prefetch limits.

Runbook: Delta in generation quality after quantization/rollout
- Reproduce on staging using the same prompt set. If regression confirmed, rollback quantized profile and open a regression alert to Applied ML and Product.

Escalation paths: pager for runtime-sre -> runtime-kernel -> applied-ml; contact list in appendix.

---

6. Release notes & upgrade guidance (summary)

This section is a live summary for major runtime releases (minor fixes not enumerated here). For full release notes see /confluence/release-notes/serving-runtime.

Recent notable releases (summary):
- 2029-09-20 (v5.4.0): Improved attention kernel with vectorized rotary support; ~12% p50 speedup on medium models. Enabled conservative rolling rollout.
- 2029-06-12 (v5.3.1): Fix for KV cache leak that caused gradual memory growth under long-context workloads.
- 2029-03-02 (v5.2.0): Introduced priority lanes and per-route batching windows.

Upgrade guidance:
1. Run full benchmark suite in staging for target models and instance types.
2. Validate p95 gate and results on eval prompts.
3. Canary rollout: 5% traffic -> 25% -> 100% with automated rollback if p95 regression >10%.
4. Monitor scheduler telemetry closely during canary window.

---

7. Known issues and mitigations (top items)

1) Intermittent p99 spikes on long-context (>=4096) for some medium models
- Symptom: occasional p99 spike with large micro-batch size.
- Mitigation: set per-route max_micro_batch_size to 8 and prefer memory-optimized kernel.

2) OOMs when enabling int4 quantized path for very large models on 48GB GPUs
- Symptom: executor crashes shortly after enabling quantized profile.
- Mitigation: enable staged rollout, reduce prefetch slices, and monitor mem_headroom; revert if OOM frequency >1/1000 requests.

3) Regression in decode throughput after attention kernel change (rare)
- Symptom: throughput AUC decreased ~18% on a subset of workloads.
- Mitigation: rollback kernel variant; maintain benchmark artifact and isolate workload pattern triggering regression.

Reporting new issues: create an issue in runtime/infra repo with labels [serving-runtime, incident, kernel] and link this doc.

Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (architecture & scheduler)
Secondary owners: runtime-kernel, eng-sre, applied-ml-and-evals

- Run bench: ./bench/run_bench.sh --model <model> --suite latency,throughput
